questions.question: How does useEffect work and when do you use it?
questions.title: Use Effect Hook
questions.direct_answer: useEffect runs side effects after render: subscriptions, timers, data fetching, DOM manipulation outside React. The dependency array controls re-running: no array = every render, [] = once after mount, [a,b] = when a or b changes (Object.is comparison). Return a cleanup function that runs before the next effect and at unmount.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: useEffect runs side effects after render: subscriptions, timers, data fetching, DOM manipulation outside React. The dependency array controls re-running: no array = every render, [] = once after mount, [a,b] = when a or b changes (Object.is comparison). Return a cleanup function that runs before the next effect and at unmount.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The lifecycle, verified:

```js
useEffect(() => {
  const conn = createConnection(roomId);  // effect: runs AFTER paint
  conn.connect();
  return () => conn.disconnect();         // cleanup: before re-effect + unmount
}, [roomId]);                             // re-run only when roomId changes
```

The three dependency-array forms:
```js
useEffect(fn);        // after EVERY render (rare — perf hazard)
useEffect(fn, []);    // once after mount, cleanup at unmount (the on-mount pattern)
useEffect(fn, [dep]); // after mount + whenever dep changes (Object.is)
```

The timing (the detail that distinguishes you): effects run AFTER the browser paints — the UI updates first, then the side effect. This is why a loading state shows before your fetch starts. If you need the effect before paint (layout measurement), useLayoutEffect is the blocking variant.

The cleanup contract (what interviewers check): every subscription needs an unsubscribe, every timer a clearTimeout, every listener a removeListener — returned as the cleanup. Missing cleanup is the #1 memory-leak and duplicate-subscription bug source. Strict Mode (dev) mounts-unmounts-remounts once to surface effects that lack cleanup.

The common mistakes: (1) object/array dependencies — a new `{}` or `[]` literal in deps is a new reference every render → infinite re-run; (2) missing deps → stale closures reading old values; (3) fetching without cleanup → race conditions when the component unmounts mid-fetch (the fix: an AbortController or an ignore flag).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[mount] --> E1[effect runs]
    U[dep changes] --> C[cleanup runs] --> E2[effect re-runs]
    UM[unmount] --> C2[cleanup runs]
    R[render] -.after paint.-> E1 & E2
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why effects exist (the design reason): rendering must be pure — same props/state, same output, no side effects inside the render body. Effects are React's escape hatch: the place where components touch the outside world (network, timers, DOM APIs, analytics). The separation lets React render concurrently (interrupt and restart renders) without half-applied side effects.

The dependency-array honesty rule (the discipline): the array must list every reactive value the effect reads — props, state, functions from component scope. The lint rule exists because omitting deps causes stale values; the correct fix is not to hide deps but to restructure: move the value into the effect, wrap stable functions in useCallback, or move logic out of the component. 'What happens if I omit it?' — the closure captures the render's value, and you get a stale-reading effect that looks like a bug.

The effect vs event distinction (the modern clarification from the React docs): effects run because the COMPONENT appeared or a dep changed — synchronization with external systems. Event handlers run because the USER did something. Code that responds to user intent belongs in handlers; code that synchronizes with the outside world (fetch on mount, subscribe to a channel) belongs in effects. Data fetching sits on the line — and the ecosystem answer is a data library (React Query, SWR) that handles caching, races, and retries better than hand-rolled effects.
